note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — TALL ARCHING BUNCH
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase describes a caespitose perennial with culms about 60–160 cm and an open panicle roughly 35–55 cm long; shorter plants also occur in regional field treatments. Use the broad arching blades, attached fine-branched head and rooted tuft together. The existing in-ground cultivated garden photograph shows the crown ABOVE soil, not excavated roots. Do not identify from a distant pale seed cloud alone.
tiles.short: Large perennial bunch with a very diffuse, often oblong panicle; trace the SAME flowering culm.
tiles.status: REAL HABIT PHOTOS — ROOTSTOCK/VOUCHER CONNECTION NOT VERIFIED

tiles.heading: 02 · HAIRY SHEATH THROAT IS NOT THE LIGULE
tiles.details: UT Williamson County treatment describes a densely ciliate true ligule about 0.4 mm, with separate 4–5 mm hairs at sheath apex/collar. Peel a fresh mature blade back and photograph the INNER junction with a 1-mm scale, distinguishing its tiny ligule from long surrounding hairs. Existing Blanco County external V-junction and sheath photos do not expose the inner membrane/hair fringe; no microscopic ligule arrow may be inferred.
tiles.short: True inner ligule ~0.4 mm; much longer 4–5 mm hairs can surround sheath throat/collar.
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — TRUE LIGULE AND DISTINCT THROAT HAIRS

tiles.heading: 03 · FOLLOW FINE BRANCHES TO INDIVIDUAL SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Kew reports an open effuse panicle with capillary sinuous branches and solitary spikelets on fine 5–15 mm pedicels. UT Williamson reports spreading pedicels about 5–13 mm on its studied material. Follow one complete attached head and photograph actual lower branch axils, individual pedicels and mature spikelets. An airy panicle alone overlaps plains and bigtop lovegrass.
tiles.short: Open oblong/ovate head; Kew panicle ~35–55 cm and pedicels ~5–15 mm.
tiles.status: GROSS BRANCHING SHOWN — MEASURED PEDICEL/AXIL PHOTO MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE MATURE MULTIFLORETED SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Photograph two or three ripe laterally compressed spikelets with a millimeter ruler, counting individual florets along one rachilla. Kew GrassBase's broad global 4–10 mm / 4–18-floret range is NOT identical to the UT Williamson County specimen treatment (~5 mm / 4–6 florets). Preserve this geographic/treatment distinction; the current source-labelled small-spikelet photo lacks calibrated floret dissection.
tiles.short: Kew ~4–10 mm, 4–18 florets; Williamson material ~5 mm and 4–6 florets.

tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT GLUMES, LEMMA AND AWNLESS TIP
tiles.details: UT Williamson describes one-veined glumes (lower 1.5–2.6 mm, upper 2–2.5(–3) mm), a three-veined fertile lemma 2.6–3.2 mm, and no lemma awn. Kew GrassBase gives broader lower-glume 1.8–4 mm, upper 1.8–3.4 mm and lemma 2.4–3.4 mm ranges. At 20–40× separate glumes, lemma and two-keeled palea; no tiny nerve, hair or glume endpoint should receive an arrow without visible resolved pixels.
tiles.short: Williamson: lower glume ~1.5–2.6 mm, upper ~2–3 mm; lemma ~2.6–3.2 mm, 3-veined, AWNLESS.

tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES + PUBLIC GATE
tiles.details: E. intermedia typically has a shorter, fine open head and relatively smoother sheath BODY; E. hirsuta has more extensive sheath-body hairs and often bearded panicle axils; E. spectabilis has a broader purple tumbling cloud. Hair placement varies, so one photo or color is insufficient. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: connected rooted Texas bunch, opened ~0.4-mm inner ligule and separate long throat hairs, whole attached panicle, lower axils, 2–3 mature spikelets dissected at scale and matched comparison sheaths. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify seven image records, nine panels, exact individual CC/NC/PD rights, all original arrows, image identities, mobile gallery and deployment. Remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Sand vs plains vs bigtop: compare sheath BODY hairs versus long THROAT hairs, then ripe spikelets.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: SAND LOVEGRASS: larger arching perennial bunch with a spacious sometimes oblong fountain of very thin panicle branches bearing small pale spikelets toward branch tips. Real archived photos show a whole tuft and scale-reference tiny separate spikelets. On fresh sheaths, longer hairs often concentrate at sheath THROAT/collar (hair fringe ligule), while nodes tend smooth; this critical collar is NOT in current photos. Compare plains and bigtop by actual sheath hair location and ripe spikelets.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Start at the actual basal growing bunch in the new CC0 Dresden garden photograph: narrow arching leaf blades converge toward a soil-level tuft. This is NOT an excavated root crown. Then use the original Texas and Sam Kieschnick images to find the fine complete panicle and real spikelets.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: UT Williamson County treatment describes a densely ciliate true ligule about 0.4 mm, with separate 4–5 mm hairs at sheath apex/collar. Peel a fresh mature blade back and photograph the INNER junction with a 1-mm scale, distinguishing its tiny ligule from long surrounding hairs. Existing Blanco County external V-junction and sheath photos do not expose the inner membrane/hair fringe; no microscopic ligule arrow may be inferred.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Kew reports an open effuse panicle with capillary sinuous branches and solitary spikelets on fine 5–15 mm pedicels. UT Williamson reports spreading pedicels about 5–13 mm on its studied material. Follow one complete attached head and photograph actual lower branch axils, individual pedicels and mature spikelets. An airy panicle alone overlaps plains and bigtop lovegrass.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Sand lovegrass combines a relatively tall persistent tuft, arching foliage and a large airy oblong panicle with throat-focused long hairs. Plains lovegrass is often shorter with less shaggy sheath body and a smaller panicle; bigtop typically bears more extensive sheath hairiness. Stinkgrass is an annual with coarser glandular reproductive parts. None of these is guaranteed from a lone distant view.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: GROWING IN SOIL · actual broad bunchgrass crown and long arching blades
panels.caption: Daderot's 2013 Dresden botanical garden photograph visibly shows a live planted bunch of sand lovegrass with many narrow arching leaves. The arrow points to the central ABOVEGROUND leafy tuft at soil level — NOT to an exposed rooted crown or rhizome. Adjacent labelled grasses are different specimens; do not confuse their blades with this plant. The true short fringe ligule (about 0.4 mm) and longer sheath-throat hairs (up to 4–5 mm) are NOT resolved.
panels.creator: Daderot
panels.modifications: Original pixels downscaled to no more than 2200px long side, RGB JPEG re-encoded EXIF/GPS-free; non-destructive separate browser arrow
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: TRUE PHOTO: sheaths and attached blades held apart, not an opened ligule
panels.caption: Sam Kieschnick's source-verified, CC BY photographed sand lovegrass from the Salado Creek Greenway in San Antonio. The narrow green blade and smoothish sheath-wrapped culm can be traced toward the fingers, but the hand partially obscures the blade/sheathed-culm transition. No 0.4-mm hair-fringed inner ligule or 4–5-mm throat hair tuft is conclusively resolved. This is a practical outside-sheath orientation view, not microscopic proof.

safety_note: The original three photographed species images now include the USDA-NRCS Texas Plant Materials Center public-domain overview (if archive succeeded) and two field views. Public-domain broad habit is not evidence for true 0.4-mm ligule fringe or lower glume. Need 10-20× collar and spikelet dissection with physical ruler. October 26: added two Research Grade, individually credited blade/sheath photos with four gross arrows. The actual inner 0.4-mm ligule and separate long 4–5-mm sheath-throat hair macro remain missing; retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS. Lane 2 2026-10-26: new regional Research Grade Cody Stricker CC BY close photograph of external blade–sheath V archived; one junction arrow added; no calibrated true ligule or whole-root connection. Do not call strict completion.
field_rule: Use size/architecture to find the candidate; do not finalize without collar anatomy and mature spikelets.
